title: Polar bonds, formal charge and resonance
note: Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½ bonding electrons. Resonance forms differ only in where π and lone-pair electrons sit; atoms never move. The real species is one hybrid that looks most like its most stable forms: full octets, little charge separation, negative charge on electronegative atoms.

read.title: Bookkeeping electrons
text: Two simple tools let you read charge from a structure. The first is electronegativity. When atoms of different electronegativity share electrons, the bond is polar: the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge. In chloromethane, chlorine pulls electron density away from carbon, leaving carbon slightly positive and ready to be attacked by electron-rich species.

The second tool is formal charge, which treats each bond as split evenly. Take valence electrons, subtract lone-pair electrons, then subtract half the bonding electrons. A nitrogen with four bonds and no lone pair, as in NH₄⁺, comes out +1. An oxygen with one bond and three lone pairs, as in hydroxide, comes out −1.

Some species cannot be drawn with a single Lewis structure. In the acetate ion, the negative charge can sit on either oxygen. Neither drawing is correct by itself; the real ion is a hybrid, and both C–O bonds have the same length. Resonance forms never move atoms, only π and lone-pair electrons. Spreading charge over several atoms lowers the energy, which is why resonance makes acetate unusually stable.
